'''John Gary Fencik''' (born June 11, 1954) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] for 12 seasons with the [[Chicago Bears]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Yale Bulldogs football|Yale Bulldogs]] and was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the 10th round of the [[1976 NFL draft]]. He was a once first-team [[All-Pro]] and twice [[Pro Bowl]] selection. Fencik is the Bears all-time leader in [[interception|interceptions.]]<ref>{{cite web |last=Mayer |first=Larry |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Tillman-repeats-stellar-performance/cd4329ee-7829-43f1-8286-e2262d28f33d |title=Tillman repeats stellar performance |publisher=[[Chicago Bears]] |access-date=October 8, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011012951/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Tillman-repeats-stellar-performance/cd4329ee-7829-43f1-8286-e2262d28f33d |archive-date=October 11, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> At the time of his retirement from the NFL, Fencik was also the Bears' all-time leader in total [[tackle (football move)|tackles]] (since surpassed by [[Mike Singletary]], then [[Brian Urlacher]]). He was also part of the [[1985 Chicago Bears season|1985 Bears team]] that won the franchise's first [[Super Bowl]] title in the [[Super Bowl XX]].

'''Gary Dennis Danielson''' (born September 10, 1951) is a former [[college football]] [[sports commentator|commentator]] and former [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]]. 

Danielson played [[college football]] for [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]] from 1969 to 1972. He led the [[Big Ten Conference]] in 1971 with a 57.8% completion percentage, 10 touchdown passes, and a 147.6 quarterback rating. 

Danielson played professional football in the [[World Football League]] in 1974 and 1975 and in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Detroit Lions]] from 1976 to 1984 and for the [[Cleveland Browns]] from 1985 to 1988. He broke the Lions' single-season record with 3,223 passing yards in 1980 and also had the second highest total to that time with 3,076 yards in 1984. At the time of his retirement, he ranked third in Lions history with 11,885 passing yards. For his career, he completed 1,105 of 1,932 passes (57.2%) for 13,764 yards, 81 touchdowns and 78 interceptions. 

Danielson began his broadcasting career at [[ESPN]] from 1990 through 1996, then [[ABC Sports]] from 1997 through 2005. In 2006, Danielson joined [[CBS Sports]] as the lead analyst for [[College Football on CBS Sports|its college football coverage]], serving in the role until his retirement at the conclusion of the 2025 season.<ref name="Retirement"></ref> Danielson received six nominations for [[Sports Emmy Awards]] throughout his broadcasting career.

'''Gary Spani''' (born January 9, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1978 to 1986. He has worked for the Chiefs' front office since 1989, and was the directors of community engagement for the Chiefs.

Spani was born in [[Satanta, Kansas]], but raised in [[Manhattan, Kansas]], and graduated from [[Manhattan High School]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas State Wildcats football|Kansas State Wildcats]]. At [[Kansas State University]], he was a three-time All [[Big Eight Conference]] selection, was conference defensive player of the year in 1977, and was named the school's first consensus [[All America]]n in 1977. He still holds the all-time tackles record for Kansas State University. Following graduation, Spani was named MVP of the [[East-West Shrine Game]].

The Chiefs selected Spani in the third round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. As a professional, Spani was a hardnosed and tenacious player. He was a [[team captain]] for the Chiefs in 1983. He formerly held the all-time tackles record for the Kansas City Chiefs, where he registered 999 career stops. His single-season record of 157 tackles with the Chiefs, set in [[1979 Kansas City Chiefs season|1979]], stood until [[2002 Kansas City Chiefs season|2002]] when it was broken by [[Mike Maslowski]]. He also recorded 9.5 sacks, recovered 10 fumbles and scored 4 touchdowns during his Chiefs career.

Spani was elected to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2002 and the Kansas City Chiefs Hall of Fame in 2003.<ref>{{College Football HoF|id=2024}}</ref>

Daughter Shalin Spani played college basketball for the Kansas State University Wildcats from 2007 to 2010.<ref>[http://www.kstatesports.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/spani_shalin00.html Shalin Spani] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120117033744/http://www.kstatesports.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/spani_shalin00.html |date=2012-01-17}} K-State Sports Women's Basketball. Retrieved November 14, 2011.</ref>  She later married K-State star quarterback and [[Heisman Trophy]] finalist [[Collin Klein]]. Daughter Taber Spani plays college basketball for the Tennessee Lady Vols.<ref>[http://www.utladyvols.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/spani_taber00.html Taber Spani] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111106015423/http://www.utladyvols.com/sports/w-baskbl/mtt/spani_taber00.html |date=2011-11-06 }} Lady Vols Basketball. Retrieved November 14, 2011.</ref> His third daughter, Tanis Spani, is a member of the Southwest Baptist University Lady Bearcat basketball team.<ref>[http://sbubearcats.com/roster.aspx?rp_id=1508] SBU Women's Basketball. Retrieved April 2, 2012.</ref>

'''Gary Keithley''' (born January 11, 1951) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] [[quarterback]] and [[Punter (football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

At Alvin High School, he was the starting quarterback for 3 years, an All-State Quarterback and he finished in the top 5 for passing yards each of his 3 seasons.<ref>{{cite web |title=Texas High School Football Records |url=https://www.pngindians.com/football/texas-high-school-football-records/ |access-date=8 August 2024}}</ref> He led the Yellowjackets to the Texas Class 3A Semifinals in 1968.

Keithley played college football at Texas in 1970 and then transferred to UTEP for his last two seasons. In 1969 he played with the freshman team at Texas. The next year he won the Southwest Conference Championship, Cotton Bowl and National Championship with Texas, but as the 3rd string QB who only threw 5 passes all season and scored a single rushing touchdown against California in the first game of the season. After some time at Alvin Junior College, he transferred to UTEP where he was the starting QB for the two seasons and set records for single-season rushing TD for quarterbacks, career completion percentage.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bloomquist |first1=Bert |title=7 things to know about the UTEP, MTSU football game on Saturday at Sun Bowl Stadium |url=https://www.elpasotimes.com/story/sports/college/utep/2018/11/09/7-things-know-utep-mtsu-game-saturday-sun-bowl-stadium/1942920002/ |access-date=8 August 2024 |date=9 November 2018}}</ref> He had 5 games with over 200 yards of passing (2 with 300+ yards) and also shared punting duties while he was at UTEP.<ref>{{cite web |title=UTEP Football Media Guide |url=https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/utepathletics.com/documents/2023/8/20/2023_UTEP_FB_Media_Guide.pdf |access-date=8 August 2024}}</ref> Keithley made the All-WAC Academic team in his senior year.<ref name="Seahawk"/>

Playing for the [[Arizona Cardinals|St. Louis Cardinals]] primarily as a backup to [[Jim Hart (American football)|Jim Hart]], he had a [[List of NFL quarterbacks who have posted a passer rating of zero|0.0 passer rating]] in each of his first two career starts in 1973, the only quarterback in NFL history to do this in back-to-back games. Despite the dubious statistic, Keithley won in his first start against the [[Atlanta Falcons]], a 32–10 victory in which he completed just two of ten passes for nine yards and an interception that was returned for a touchdown.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cunningham|first=George|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/64931017/|title=Falcons Die Again in December, 32-10|newspaper=[[The Atlanta Journal and Constitution]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 10, 1973|access-date=December 16, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/64931999/|title=Falcons' Wild-Card Hopes Jolted in Upset to Cards|agency=[[Associated Press|AP]]|newspaper=[[Tallahassee Democrat]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 10, 1973|access-date=December 16, 2020}}</ref> The following year, Keithley lost his backup role to [[Dennis Shaw]], who played for Cardinals head coach [[Don Coryell]] in college, while his punting duties were reassigned to rookie punter Hal Roberts.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ingram|first=Bob|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/64951332/|title=Lonely Sidelines|newspaper=[[El Paso Herald-Post]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 24, 1974|access-date=December 16, 2020}}</ref> Still with the Cardinal in 1974 and 1975, he never played those two seasons. He was picked up by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the 1976 expansion draft but did not make the roster.<ref name="Seahawk">{{cite web|url=http://www.beckys-place.com/keithley.html|title=Gary Keithley was there!|last=Thiel|first=Doug|access-date=September 9, 2021}}</ref>

He was the backup quarterback of the [[BC Lions]] in 1977 and 1978.

Keithley became a high school football coach. He was the Offensive Coordinator at Cleburne High Schools starting in 1996 and then became the head coach for 4 years starting in 1997. He coached the team to the playoffs in 2002 and served as the Cleburne ISD's Athletic Director before retiring in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brandon |first1=George |title=Pigskin spy story rocks Cleburne |url=https://greekchat.com/gcforums/showthread.php?t=57339 |publisher=Dallas Morning News |access-date=8 August 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Magers |first1=Lisa |title=Former athletic director named to Alvin hall of fame |url=https://beckys-place.com/keithley.html |publisher=Cleburne Times-Review |access-date=8 August 2024}}</ref>

In 2009 he was in the inaugural class for the Alvin ISD Athletic Hall of Honor.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Collins |first1=Stephen |title=AISD releases inaugural class for Athletic Hall of Honor |url=https://www.alvinsun.net/sports/article_8289b3eb-8e53-5671-b2b4-4c739c0b5938.html |access-date=8 August 2024 |date=29 October 2019}}</ref>

His son Gary Keithley Jr. was drafted by the [[New York Yankees]] in the 33rd round of the 2003 MLB June Amateur Draft, but never played professional baseball at any level.
